working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses and UK Conditions
angle: A practical, opinionated decision guide for the regular UK club golfer who is weighing up whether the extra cost and weight of an electric trolley is genuinely worth it for the courses they play, rather than a straight product round-up. Frames the choice around UK-specific factors: hilly parkland, soft winter ground, small car boots, and how often you actually play.
research_notes:
- Core split: electric trolleys carry the bag under battery power (you steer); push trolleys require the golfer to push manually. Key trade-off is cost and weight vs effort saved.
- Terrain is the decisive factor for UK golfers: hilly or undulating courses strongly favour electric; flatter municipal/links courses are well-served by a decent push trolley.
- Electric trolleys are heavier due to motor, battery, and gearbox — meaningful when lifting in and out of a car boot every week.
- Lithium batteries are now standard on reputable electric models; an 18-hole battery covers a standard round, 27/36-hole batteries suit hillier or back-to-back rounds.
- Downhill control (DHC on Motocaddy, similar on others) is a genuinely useful feature on soft, sloping UK ground — not just a marketing add-on.
- Three-wheel push trolleys are easier on the body than old two-wheel pull models — pushing weight ahead rather than dragging it behind.
- Push trolleys: typically under £200 for a quality model; no charging required; simpler to maintain. Electric: entry-level around £500+, premium GPS models £1,000+.
- Folded size matters for UK golfers with smaller car boots — both categories now have compact-fold options but push trolleys remain easier to store.
- Key brands active in UK market: PowaKaddy (FX and CT ranges for electric; Micra for push), Motocaddy (S1, M5 GPS DHC for electric; QB2 for push), Clicgear (4.0 push — aircraft-grade aluminium construction, braking system), Big Max (Blade IP 2 push — FlatFold mechanism).
- Playing frequency matters: once or twice a month on a flat course = push trolley sufficient; regular weekly play on demanding ground = electric pays back in comfort over a season.
- Features worth considering on electric: speed control, downhill braking, all-terrain tyres. Features to skip unless you'll actually use them: GPS integration on the handle, remote/follow modes (significant price jump).
- Wheel size on push trolleys matters for UK conditions: larger rear wheels (10–12 inch) handle wet, muddy ground better than smaller (7–8 inch) wheels.
- Storage considerations: electric trolleys should be stored dry and charged per battery guidance to protect battery life.
